prime.problem: Using the biggest model for every call in an agent means every "is this JSON valid?" step pays a big model's start, speed and price. Using the smallest means hard steps fail. Neither size fits every call.
prime.fits: Last agent card, the lever that touches both sides of the fraction. Compounding errors showed checks turn failures into cheap retries; routing uses those same checks to escalate from a small model to a big one.
prime.goal: Design a routing rule for an agent and compute its time and cost against using one model everywhere.

attend: What makes a small model faster per call: the start, the speed, or both?
Why does the routed plan still spend 22.4 s of its 37.9 s on the three hard calls?
Why is asking a model which model to use a poor router?
Why does switching models mid-conversation throw away prompt caching?

must: Smaller models start sooner and write faster (Haiku 0.68 s, 89 t/s vs Opus 2.94 s, 62 t/s) and cost less → easy calls don't need the big model's intelligence → route easy steps small
A small model fails some steps → a cheap check (tests, schema, parse) catches the miss → the call re-runs on a bigger model → one escalation costs one extra call (2.91 s) but keeps the task correct
Hard calls dominate the routed time → routing helps most when the model gap is wide and most calls are easy → for hard, ambiguous steps just use the big model
elevated: The stored prompt state (KV cache) belongs to the model that built it → a switched model re-reads its prompt from scratch → give the small model a short, self-contained prompt, not the full history
reference: the three models' prices and Intelligence Index values
the illustrative 7/3 split and token counts

compress.prompt: From memory, write the per-call time and cost formulas, compute one easy call on Haiku and one on Sonnet, and explain in two sentences how routing plus escalation keeps the task correct. Add when not to route.
checklist: time = TTFT + output tokens ÷ speed; cost = (in × $in + out × $out) ÷ 1M
a check catches a small-model miss and escalates it
don't route hard reasoning, unclear bugs or steps that steer the rest of the loop

retrieve.q: Explain why routing needs a check to be safe, and what happens without one.
answer: the small model will get some steps wrong
a check catches the miss so the step re-runs on a bigger model
without a check, the wrong step passes silently and compounds

retrieve.q: Walk through the routed plan's time: which calls ran where, and how the 37.9 s adds up.
answer: 1 easy call failed and re-ran on Sonnet: + 2.91 s, total ≈ 37.9 s

retrieve.q: Your agent has 10 calls, only 2 of them easy. Is routing worth building? What if 9 were easy?
answer: 2 easy: small savings, plus a router and two models to test: probably not
9 easy: most calls get faster and cheaper: worth it
either way, weigh the escalation rate and the lost prompt cache

compare.q: Raising effort and escalating to a bigger model are both ways to spend more on a hard step. Which one changes the tokens and which the model, and which keeps the prompt cache?
answer: effort: same model, more hidden tokens; the cache is kept
escalation: a different model; its cache starts empty
effort is simpler to switch per call; a bigger model raises the ceiling on what's solvable

compare.q: Model routing picks which model answers a call; a serving router picks which replica runs a request. What is each one optimising, and what does each need to know?
answer: model routing: quality vs time/cost per call; needs step difficulty and a check
replica routing: load and cache locality across copies of one model; needs queue lengths and prefix hits
both trade a small decision cost for better use of expensive capacity

predict.q: In the routed plan, suppose 3 of the 7 easy calls fail the check and escalate instead of 1. Predict whether routing still beats all-Sonnet on time and on cost. Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: Time: 7 × 1.80 + 3 × 7.45 + 3 × 2.91 ≈ 43.7 s, now slower than all-Sonnet's 42.7 s. Cost: $0.0245 + $0.072 + 3 × $0.007 ≈ $0.118, still slightly cheaper than $0.121. A high escalation rate erases the time win first.

apply.task: List the calls in an agent task you run and label each easy or hard, with a check (or none). Using the three-model table, compute the time and cost for all-Sonnet, all-Haiku (with your guess of how many steps fail) and a routed plan with your expected escalations. Find the escalation rate at which routing stops saving time.
apply.done: You have three totals computed with the per-call formulas and a break-even escalation count for time.
apply.hint: Each escalation adds a Sonnet easy call: 2.91 s and $0.0070. In the card's split, routing stops saving time at 3 escalations out of 7.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how many escalations erase the time win?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the cache doesn't carry over between models?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: check → escalation, or escalation rate → net saving?
Which steps in your own agent are clearly easy, and what would check them?
Which agent card's lever would you apply before routing, and why?
